title: Cry Wolf
full_review:
In 2002, University of Southern California film school graduate Jeff Wadlow won a contest sponsored by the Chrysler Corp. for his short film "Living the Lie." The prize included $1 million and a chance to direct a feature film.

The result is "Cry Wolf" (Rogue), a modestly involving teen thriller set in a posh prep school, where a group of students (including Lindy Booth and Jared Padalecki) initiate a new arrival (Julian Morris) into their clique. The preppy pack meets late at night to play a clandestine version of "truth or dare" in the school's musty chapel.

The film opens with the off-campus murder of a town local, brutally shot in the woods at night by an unseen assailant. The unsolved crime has everyone nervous.

As a prank, the group concocts a story about a masked killer -- "the Wolf" -- and posts it on the school's intranet site, issuing ominous rumors that his next victim will be a student.

The hoax is blown by their journalism teacher (an unconvincing Jon Bon Jovi), so when they find themselves being menaced by a real stalker -- eerily echoing their fabrications -- no one believes them (thus the title).

In light of the film's themes of truth and lies, its ads are a bit of a deception. With its foreboding ski-mask imagery, the poster would suggest a "Friday the 13th"-style horror flick. It's not. Be warned, however, that the movie does contain some of those elements, though by comparison they are relatively restrained (but still a bit intense for a PG-13 film).

As directed by Wadlow, the low-budget film's "Ten Little Indians" story line is reasonably suspenseful despite genre cliches, and its better-than-average script -- littered with red herrings and capped with a surprise twist -- that emphasizes psychological tension over slasher gore.

The film has some bloody violence, sexual humor and suggestiveness, and sporadic crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
